headline: Fort Trumbull rip still working the ebb, but you'll need first light to find willing bass
subhead: Snapper blues have taken over the upper river while stripers slide into the low-light hours as the Thames warms into the high 60s.
body_markdown:
There's a spot off Fort Trumbull where the current pinches between the point and the channel edge, and on a good outgoing tide you can watch the seam stand up like a fence line in the water — smooth on one side, nervous and boiling on the other. That seam has been the tell all week. Bass are still using it, but they're not holding in it the way they were three weeks ago when the water had more push and less heat. Now they're ghosting through on the tail end of the ebb, usually the last ninety minutes before dead low, and then dropping back down into deeper water once the sun gets up over the fort walls.

Water in the harbor and lower river has settled into the high 60s, which sounds cool for mid-August until you remember what this river was running back in July. It's enough heat that the bass have gone the way stripers always go when the thermometer creeps up on them — they've pushed their feeding into the dark hours and the gray hours, dawn and dusk, and gone quiet and lazy through the heat of the day. I fished the sub base pilings at 5:45 Tuesday morning on the last of the outgoing and had three fish in twenty minutes on a white 3/4-ounce bucktail bounced tight to the concrete, then nothing for the next hour once the sun cleared the trees. That's the window right now. Don't sleep through it.

Gold Star Bridge is still doing what it always does this time of year — holding fish in the shadow line on the downriver side of the pilings, especially on the bottom third of the tide when the current is still moving enough to keep bait pinned against the structure. Live eels have been the difference-maker there for anyone willing to fish them slow and let the current do the work instead of retrieving. Umbrella rigs and swimming plugs have taken a few too, but nothing you'd call consistent — this is more of a "put your time in and pick off two or three quality fish" bite than a blitz.

Upriver, it's a different story entirely, and a louder one. Snapper blues are thick from around the Poquonnock confluence right down through the flats above the bridge, chewing through schools of peanut bunker with the kind of reckless enthusiasm only a one-pound bluefish can manage. We flagged this building two weeks back, and it's held true — the juvenile blues haven't thinned out, they've thickened, and there's every reason to think some of these fish start pushing into adult class as we roll into September. If you've got kids or you just want steady bent-rod action, small silver spoons or Kastmasters on light spinning gear will keep you busy for hours up there. Down at the river mouth and along the harbor edge, the adult blues mixing with the stripers are running three to four pounds, occasionally bigger, and they'll hit the same bucktails and swim shads you're throwing for bass — which makes for some pleasant surprises and the occasional bitten-off leader.

Porgy fishing has been the most dependable thing going on the harbor structure and breakwaters — New London breakwater, the rocks off Pleasure Beach, anywhere there's a hard bottom edge in fifteen to twenty-five feet. Sandworms and clam on a simple high-low rig, fished on the bottom stages of the tide when the current slows enough to hold your bait in the strike zone, has been producing steady catches of porgies in the ten-to-twelve-inch range with enough larger fish mixed in to keep it interesting. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's the kind of thing you can count on when the bass get finicky.

Blackfish are still mostly a non-story right now — the summer stretch is typically quiet for them in this system, and I haven't heard of anyone targeting them seriously until the water starts cooling in September and pushes them back onto the rockier structure around Fort Trumbull and the breakwaters. That's a fall conversation, not an August one.

Tide-wise, we're coming off the strong new-moon push and easing into the softer first-quarter cycle, which explains some of the drop-off in aggression at spots like Fort Trumbull — less current means less concentrated bait, means less reason for a bass to commit in daylight. That'll start rebuilding again as we approach the August 28 full moon, and when it does, I'd expect the harbor and river mouth bite to sharpen back up, especially if any push of adult bunker works its way down from the Sound the way it has further east along the coast this month. If that bait shows up in the river mouth, it could trigger the kind of aggressive, more prolonged bass activity we're seeing from Narragansett up toward Plymouth right now — worth watching for.

For this week: fish the early and late tide stages, work Fort Trumbull and the sub base pilings on the last of the ebb, and don't discount the porgy grounds if the bass go quiet on you. If the moon builds the current back up like I expect, I'd start checking the river mouth for signs of bunker showing before the full moon hits.
